# Why HTML Forms Don't Submit via PUT Without a CSRF Token You have defined your routes correctly, mapping `PUT post/{post}` to `postcontroller@update`. Your form action points to the correct URI (`/post/{postID}`), and the method attribute is set to `put`. However, the submission fails. This isn't an issue with CSS styling or URL construction; it is a fundamental security constraint in modern web frameworks: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection. ### The Security Mechanism By default, Laravel disables support for unsafe HTTP methods like `PUT`, `PATCH`, and `DELETE` on specific routes unless the request includes a valid CSRF token. This mechanism prevents malicious websites from tricking authenticated users into modifying data on your site without their consent. When you use a standard `
` tag with `method="put"`, the browser sends the request directly to the server. If your route has not been explicitly whitelisted or if no CSRF token is present in the payload, Laravel's middleware will reject the request before your controller method ever executes. This explains why "it doesn't work"âthe server responds with a `419` (Page Expired) or `405` (Method Not Allowed), and you likely see no output because the redirect happens immediately. ### The Traditional Solution: Form Helpers The most common recommendation is to use Blade's form helpers, such as `{{ Form::put(...) }}`. While this generates the correct HTML structure automatically, it abstracts away the ability to apply custom CSS classes directly to the input elements or the form container itself in older versions of Laravel. If your primary requirement is maintaining full control over CSS stylingâperhaps using Bootstrap or a custom stylesheetâthe helper approach feels restrictive because the generated markup is static once rendered. ### The Modern Approach: Manual Token Injection In modern Laravel applications (specifically version 5.2 and above), you can safely use raw HTML forms with custom styling by manually injecting the CSRF token into your `` tag. This gives you complete freedom over CSS classes while satisfying security requirements. You need to ensure two things in your view: 1. The `method` attribute is set to `put`. 2. A hidden input field containing the session-based CSRF token exists within the form body. Here is how to implement this with full CSS control: ```html @csrf

When Laravel's middleware intercepts the incoming request, it extracts this token and compares it against the one stored in your user's session. If they match, the `postcontroller@update` method executes successfully. If you are using an older version of Laravel where `@csrf` might not be available or configured differently, you can manually insert the token using the `old_input` helper or directly accessing the session: ```html ``` ### Styling Considerations By using the raw `
` tag with manual class application (as shown in the example above), you bypass the limitations of the Form helpers. You can now wrap the form in a custom container, apply specific padding to the `.edit-btn` class, or use grid systems that require specific class names on the parent div without worrying about how the helper generates them. Just remember to include `{{ old('post', $post->post) }}` (as seen in the textarea example) to preserve the data if the validation fails and the user needs to correct their input. Without this, a failed validation would clear the form, forcing the user to retype their content. ### Summary of Actions To fix your issue while retaining CSS flexibility: 1. Keep your existing `` structure with `action` and `method`. 2. Insert the `@csrf` directive immediately inside the opening `` tag. 3. Ensure your view file is being rendered by Blade (`.blade.php`). Once the CSRF token is present in the request payload, Laravel will treat the `PUT` request as legitimate, allowing your `post.update` action to execute without error.
